newsitem.title: USA: Chrysler offers shift lock device for Jeeps.
newsitem.headline: Chrysler offers shift lock device for Jeeps.

text.p: Chrysler Corp. on Tuesday offered to install a "brake-park" device on 2 million older sport utility vehicles -- a move safety advocates called a pre-emptive strike against a growing number of sudden acceleration complaints.

Chrysler said it is taking the action to cut down on the possibility of what it called "pedal misapplication" by drivers who mistakenly step on the accelerator instead of the brake, causing the vehicle to suddenly move.

Company officials stressed the move is not a recall. It comes two years after the U.S. National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) pressured the automaker to replace rear latches in 4.5 million 1984-95 minivans after complaints surfaced that the original latches were not strong enough to hold rear doors closed after an impact.
NHTSA officials said Tuesday that Chrysler took the brake-park action on its own without pressure from the safety agency.

There are 1.3 million 1984-95 Cherokees and 700,000 1993-95 Grand Cherokees involved in the retrofit of a brake-park shift interlock package said Chrysler, the No. 3 U.S. automaker. The interlocks require the driver to press the brake pedal before shifting into drive or reverse.
Safety proponents claimed Chrysler is trying to head off a situation where it is forced to recall the vehicles because of an increasing number of injuries.

"The number of injuries, the number of accidents has reached the boiling point, and this is absolutely a pre-emptive action on Chrysler's behalf," said Sean Cane, vice president of Ralph Hoar & Associates, a safety group.

Cane said there have been a number of high-profile incidents, including the death of a doctor in the Chicago area last month, where Chrysler sport utility vehicles have suddenly lurched forward or backward.

The incidents have begun to draw attention from news and other organisations said Cane. Last year, the International Carwash Association issued a special alert warning about persisting problems with Jeep Cherokees "lurching" when they come off washing lines.

The NHTSA said it has received notice of five fatalities, 151 injuries and 175 crashes because of unintended acceleration involving the Cherokee and Grand Cherokee in the 1993-96 model years. All told, Chrysler and NHTSA have received 546 complaints of unintended acceleration regarding those two vehicles in 1993-96 model years.
Ken Weinstein, associate administrator for safety and assurance, said through a spokeswoman the safety agency feels Chrysler's action is "appropriate," and plans to continue to monitor the situation.
Chrysler said it has concluded incidents of sudden acceleration are being caused by drivers mistakenly stepping on the accelerator rather than the brake.

"We have carefully examined 'unintended acceleration' reports and our investigations have never revealed any evidence of throttle, electronic engine management system or brake system malfunction," Susan Cischke, executive director of Vehicle Certification, Compliance and Safety Affairs for Chrysler, said in a statement.
Chrysler said 1996 and 1997 model year versions of the Cherokee and Grand Cherokee have the brake-park shift interlock. No other Chrysler vehicles have the interlocks.
Officials at Ford Motor Co. and General Motors Corp. said all of their vehicles with automatic transmissions have had the interlocks for several years.

Chrysler spokesman Jason Vines would not disclose the projected cost of the retrofit, other than to say it would be a "substantial amount of money." Dealers will need between 30 minutes to one hour to complete the job.

The automaker will begin alerting owners in late summer. The company expects more than half of 1990-95 model year owners to take advantage of the programme, said Vines, although the follow-through rate for older vehicles will probably be less.
